newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania govt says will not sign pyramid fund law.
newsitem.headline: Albania govt says will not sign pyramid fund law.

text.p: Political infighting in Albania intensified on Wednesday, just days ahead of a general election, when the government said it would not countersign a presidential decree to regulate shady investment schemes.
The move dimmed prospects for a speedy resolution of the crisis that has engulfed Albania, Europe's poorest country, following the collapse of five such funds earlier this year.

President Sali Berisha, responding to urgent pleas from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, on Tuesday approved legislation to control the schemes and quell social unrest in the Balkan nation.

But Finance Minister Arben Malaj, a member of the Socialist Party challenging Berisha's Democratic Party in Sunday's poll, told a news conference the government had no intention of signing the decree.
Berisha, he said, had altered several key aspects of the draft presented by Albania's multi-party interim government.
"We cannot sign the decree which (represents) a change from the original draft presented by the government. All the changes should first be approved by the government," Malaj said.

The breakdown of the five pyramid investment schemes sparked a wave of violence in which some 1,500 people died. The Socialists are now in government after a coalition administration was formed in March.
Malaj said there was little chance the political stand-off could be resolved before Sunday's elections, widely seen as the only hope for restoring peace in Albania.
"There were very good odds to have this law approved before the elections," he said. "But I really cannot be held responsible for the president's actions."

The decree was aimed at establishing clearer rules for setting up investment funds and monitoring their activities. It also provided for domestic as well as international auditors to oversee their day-to-day business.

Malaj said Berisha had deleted references outlining the exact procedures governing the appointment of the auditors. The president also wanted the finance minister personally to be in charge of monitoring the success of the legislation rather than the government as a whole, he added.

According to government estimates, at least $1.2 billion in savings was wiped out when the five schemes, in which interest to old depositors was paid with deposits from new investors, collapsed at the start of the year.

Malaj said Berisha's Democrats had ignored calls to reign in the funds, which offered huge rates of return to investors with little awareness of market economics after 45 years under one of the world's harshest Stalinist regimes.
"The government was aware (of the problem) since 1995 and if it had intervened, the consequences would now be much smaller and the amount of money lost not as big," Malaj said.
